title: Review: The Haber process and the use of NPK fertilisers (chemistry only); Key ideas

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Group
items.clue: A vertical column of the periodic table.

items.label: Atom
items.clue: The tiny particle from which all matter is composed.

items.label: Triple superphosphate
items.clue: The calcium phosphate made by treating phosphate rock with phosphoric acid.

items.label: Proton transfer
items.clue: A reaction in which a hydrogen ion, H+, moves from one substance to another.

questions.stem: A strip of zinc is placed in copper sulfate solution. The blue colour fades and copper is deposited on the zinc. Which of the three ways of reacting is this?

options.text: Electron sharing, because zinc and copper share electrons here.
Proton transfer, because zinc gives protons to copper ions.
No transfer at all; the copper simply drops out of solution.
Electron transfer, because zinc atoms lose electrons to copper ions.

questions.explanation: Zn loses two electrons to become Zn2+, and Cu2+ gains them to become copper metal, so this is electron transfer.

questions.stem: Which of these changes is an example of electron sharing?

options.text: Two hydrogen atoms bond together to form a hydrogen molecule.
Sodium and chlorine atoms react to form solid sodium chloride.
A magnesium atom loses two electrons and becomes an ion.
An acid reacts with an alkali to give a salt and water.

questions.explanation: Two non-metal atoms bond by sharing a pair of electrons, which forms the covalent bond in H2.

questions.stem: What does it mean to say that energy is conserved in chemical reactions?

options.text: Reactions that give out heat create the energy that they release.
Energy is neither created nor destroyed, only transferred.
Energy is gradually used up, which is why reactions stop.
Reactions that take energy in destroy some of what they absorb.

questions.explanation: This is the principle stated in the specification: energy is conserved, so a reaction can only move energy between stores.

questions.stem: During a reaction in an open beaker, the mixture and the beaker both become noticeably hotter. What has happened to the energy?

options.text: The reaction has created new energy as the products formed.
Some of the energy was destroyed as the new bonds formed.
It has all been transferred out to the surroundings.
Some of it was used up as the reaction took place.

questions.explanation: The reaction is exothermic: energy stored in the chemicals has been transferred out to the mixture, the beaker and the air, which is conservation, not creation.

questions.stem: A student makes ammonium sulfate in the laboratory by titration and crystallisation. How does industrial production of the same salt differ?

options.text: It reacts the ammonia with an alkali rather than an acid
It is carried out in exactly the same way, but with larger apparatus
It runs continuously on a large scale, with reactants recycled
It adds phosphorus and potassium to make the compound NPK

questions.explanation: Industrial production is continuous, large scale and integrated, whereas the laboratory prepares a single small batch.

questions.stem: Magnesium burns in oxygen to form magnesium oxide, MgO. What happens to electrons as this compound forms?

options.text: Each magnesium atom shares its two electrons with an oxygen atom.
Each oxygen atom transfers two electrons to a magnesium atom.
Each magnesium atom transfers two electrons to an oxygen atom.
Each magnesium atom gives two protons to an oxygen atom.

questions.explanation: Magnesium has two outer electrons to lose and oxygen needs two to fill its outer shell, giving Mg2+ and O2- ions in MgO.

questions.stem: Ammonia from the Haber process can be used to manufacture which substances?

options.text: Ammonium salts and nitric acid
Ammonium salts and sulfuric acid
Nitric acid and sulfuric acid
Nitric acid and a compound called NPK

questions.explanation: The specification states that ammonia can be used to manufacture ammonium salts and nitric acid.

questions.stem: The key ideas state that there are barriers to reaction. What does this mean?

options.text: Reacting particles are kept apart by a physical layer between them.
Substances have to be melted before their particles can react.
Colliding particles need a minimum amount of energy before they react.
Every collision between particles will produce a reaction.

questions.explanation: The barrier is an energy requirement. Collisions below that energy do not lead to reaction, so different barriers give different rates.

questions.stem: Which salt is produced when phosphate rock is treated with phosphoric acid?

options.text: Calcium phosphate, called triple superphosphate
Calcium sulfate, the salt in single superphosphate
Calcium phosphate mixed with some calcium sulfate
Ammonium phosphate, made from the rock alone

questions.explanation: Phosphoric acid converts phosphate rock into calcium phosphate, known as triple superphosphate.

questions.stem: What does it mean to say that the elements show periodic relationships in their properties?

options.text: Properties change smoothly from the first element to the last one.
Only physical properties such as melting point follow a pattern.
Similar properties recur at regular intervals across the table.
Elements sharing a period have very similar properties.

questions.explanation: Periodic means repeating: as the elements are listed in order, similar chemical and physical properties reappear at regular intervals.

questions.stem: Phosphate rock is treated with nitric acid. Which products are formed?

options.text: Ammonium nitrate and calcium oxide
Phosphoric acid and calcium nitrate
Calcium phosphate and calcium sulfate
Calcium nitrate and calcium oxide

questions.explanation: Treating phosphate rock with nitric acid produces phosphoric acid and calcium nitrate.

questions.stem: Two different reactions are carried out at the same temperature and concentration, but one goes much more slowly than the other. What best explains the difference?

options.text: A physical barrier keeps its particles apart in the flask.
The slower reaction releases less energy overall than the faster.
Its particles are colliding much less often than the other.
The slower reaction has the higher energy barrier to overcome.

questions.explanation: A higher barrier means a smaller fraction of collisions carry enough energy to react, so fewer collisions succeed and the rate is lower.
